paragraph: SS-1 USS Holland was the Navy's first submarine. Designer John Holland began sketching submarine designs as early as 1869 and built five experimental submarines between 1878 and 1895 before arriving at the more successful Holland design. The vessel included all the major components of a modern submarine: dual propulsion systems, a fixed center of gravity, separate main and auxiliary ballast systems, a hydrodynamic shape, and a modern weapons system.

paragraph: USS Plunger (SS-2) was an Adder Class submarine torpedo boat laid down on 21 May 1901 at Crescent Shipyard, Elizabethport, N.J. She was launched on 1 February 1902 and commissioned on 19 September 1903. On 25 August 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt dove aboard the vessel off Long Island Sound, spending three hours underwater. The submarine was renamed USS A-1 on 17 November 1911 and was struck from the Naval Register on 24 February 1913. After being designated Target E on 29 August 1916, she was sold for scrapping on 26 January 1922.

paragraph: SS-163 USS Barracuda was a B type submarine built at Portsmouth Navy Yard and commissioned in 1925. She displaced 2000 tons surfaced and 2,506 tons submerged, with a length of 341'6", beam of 27'1", and draft of 14'7". The submarine achieved speeds of 18 knots surfaced and 11 knots submerged, with a range of 10,000 miles at 11 knots surfaced. Her armament consisted of 1 5"/51 gun, 4 bow and 2 stern torpedo tubes, and 12 21" torpedoes. She carried a complement of 80 crew members.

paragraph: USS Gato (SS-212) was the lead ship of the Gato-class submarines. Named after a species of small catshark found in waters along the west coast of Mexico, her keel was laid on 5 October 1940 and she was launched on 21 August 1941. Gato was commissioned on 31 December 1941 and decommissioned on 16 March 1946. She later served as a Naval Reserve Training vessel before being placed out of service and struck from the Naval Register on 1 March 1960. Gato was sold for scrap on 25 July 1960.

paragraph: USS Balao (SS-285) was a Balao-class submarine built at Portsmouth Navy Yard in Kittery, Maine. Her keel was laid on 26 June 1942, she was launched on 27 October 1942, and she was commissioned on 4 February 1943. The submarine displaced 1,526 tons surfaced and 2,424 tons submerged, measured 311 feet in length, and could reach 20 knots surfaced and 9 knots submerged. Armament included 6 bow and 4 stern torpedo tubes with 24 torpedoes. She carried a crew complement of 80. USS Balao was decommissioned on 20 August 1946.

paragraph: USS Tench (SS-417) was the lead ship of the Tench-class submarines. Built at Portsmouth Navy Yard, her keel was laid on 1 April 1944, she was launched on 7 July 1944, and commissioned on 6 October 1944. The submarine displaced 1,570 tons surfaced and 2,414 tons submerged, measured 311'8" in length, and was armed with 6 bow and 4 stern torpedo tubes carrying 24 torpedoes. She was reclassified as AGSS-417 on October 1, 1969, decommissioned on May 8, 1970, and struck from the Naval Register on August 16, 1973.

paragraph: USS Tang (SS-563) was the second ship to bear the name Tang. Her keel was laid on 18 April 1949 at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, she was launched on 19 June 1951, and commissioned on 25 October 1951. The new Tang introduced the fast attack concept to the submarine community with its streamlined hull, integrated snorkel system, and increased speed and depth. She was described as the first of the modern fast attack submarines and surrogate parent of the U.S. Navy's nuclear power submarine force. In 1980, USS Tang was decommissioned as the oldest diesel-electric submarine in the Navy and the last operational one in the Atlantic Fleet.

paragraph: USS Albacore (AGSS-569) was an experimental submarine that represented a radical change in submarine design. Designed, built, and maintained by Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, Albacore was launched on August 1st, 1953 and served as a research submarine until 1972. The hull was designed with underwater speed as the prime requirement, and it was built with newly developed high-strength steel (HY-80). The vessel pioneered the teardrop-shaped hull and featured a true underwater hull of cylindrical shape that has become the standard for today's submarines worldwide.

paragraph: USS Skipjack (SSN-585) was a Skipjack-class nuclear attack submarine built by General Dynamics Electric Boat Division in Groton, Connecticut. Her keel was laid on 29 May 1956, she was launched on 26 May 1958, and commissioned on 15 April 1959. The submarine had a surface displacement of 3,075 tons and a submerged displacement of 3,513 tons. She was decommissioned on 19 April 1990 and struck from the Naval Register the same day. The vessel was disposed of through the Nuclear-Powered Ship and Submarine Recycling Program on 17 March 1996.

paragraph: USS Thresher (SSN-593) was a nuclear-powered attack submarine and the lead ship of a new class of fast-attack submarine. Her keel was laid down at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, ME in 1958. The submarine was the culmination of twelve years of scientific and engineering research to develop a submarine hunter-killer to address the threat that Soviet submarines posed. USS Thresher was lost on April 10, and a search was subsequently conducted for the vessel.

The majority of Sturgeon's Cold War operations were classified. Sturgeon-class submarines were the workhorses of the Submarine Force during the Cold War. The sail of USS Sturgeon is currently on exhibit outdoors at the Naval Undersea Museum.

paragraph: SSN-774 USS Virginia is a nuclear-powered attack submarine and the lead ship of the Virginia class. USS Virginia (SSN 774) was first commissioned in 2004. The Navy has been procuring Virginia-class submarines since FY1998, and the class replaces the aging fleet of Los Angeles-class attack submarines. SSN-774 is equipped with VLS for 12 Tomahawk missiles. By the start of FY2026, 26 Virginia-class boats were in service.

paragraph: SSBN-598 USS George Washington was the world's first nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine. The designation SSBN means Ship Submersible Ballistic (Nuclear), with "Nuclear" referring to the ship's propulsive power. On 15 November 1960, USS George Washington deployed on its first strategic patrol carrying 16 Polaris A1 missiles. The submarine returned from patrol on 21 January 1961, coming alongside the tender USS Proteus at New London, Connecticut. In the early 1980s, SSBN-598 George Washington had its missiles removed and was reclassified as an attack submarine, a role in which it served for several years prior to decommissioning.

paragraph: USS Ethan Allen (SSBN-608) was a ballistic missile submarine commissioned in August 1961. She was the sixth ballistic missile submarine commissioned by the U.S. Navy in the span of three years and served as the lead ship of the Navy's second class of ballistic missile submarines. Ethan Allen and her sister SSBNs were the product of the Cold War arms race, a competition between the United States and Soviet Union to design and build increasingly sophisticated nuclear weapons.

paragraph: SSBN-616 USS Lafayette was a Lafayette Class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine built at the Electric Boat Division of General Dynamics in Groton, Connecticut. Her keel was laid on 17 January 1961, and she was launched on 8 May 1962 with First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy serving as sponsor. The submarine was commissioned on 23 April 1963. She served as a Polaris missile submarine during the Cold War. USS Lafayette was decommissioned and struck from the Naval Register on 12 August 1991, with recycling completed on 25 February 1992 at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard.
